sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Málaga is tightening car access through a low-emission zone and a new street-parking tax. The Sustainable Mobility ordinance, in force since 30 November 2024, regulates a 437-hectare Zona de Bajas Emisiones (ZBE) controlled by licence-plate recognition, so drivers do not need to display a label [0][2]. Access is phased by year. In the first year, all vehicles could circulate. From 30 November 2025, cars and motorbikes with no environmental label had to be domiciled in Málaga to enter. From 30 November 2026 the same limit extends to label B vehicles [0][1]. In June 2026 the Andalusian High Court annulled the access regulation because it treated vehicles domiciled in the city differently from those of other municipalities. The report said the city would study the ruling without ruling out an appeal, and that the ruling was not final [3]. We do not know the outcome.

On the street, the regulated parking (SARE) is now a tax. Since 1 January 2026 the general rate is €1.00 an hour, with a minimum of €0.50 per 30 minutes and a maximum of €2.50 for 150 minutes. Residents pay €0.20 per 24 hours. Overstaying costs €5.00 and parking without a ticket €9.00, in both cases if regularised voluntarily within three days [9]. The municipal parking company SMASSA became fully publicly owned on 30 December 2024, when the city bought the 49% held by Unicaja and Empark, and began a merger procedure with the EMT bus company in January 2025 [10].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
SMASSA's network is large. A 2023 city release says it has promoted 53 car parks in the city's neighbourhoods with more than 14,140 resident spaces, including 11 mixed car parks and La Marina as rotation-only [11]. The Pío Baroja car park in Echeverría del Palo, with 276 rotation spaces, cost more than €11 million and was commissioned in March 2024 [12]. New supply is planned at the edge. A surface car park with 135 rotation spaces was presented for Baños del Carmen in June 2026 [15], the city awarded a study of a park-and-ride near the Totalán stream and has finished one next to the Martín Carpena sports palace [16], and a preliminary proposal there suggests 467 spaces for €20 to 23 million, plus €6 to 14 million for access works [17]. A provisional 750-space paid car park at the Hospital Civil was due to open on 25 August 2026, and we have not confirmed that it opened [18]. A plan to extend the Palacio de Ferias y Congresos on a parking plot includes two underground floors of about 2,000 spaces, and has so far had only initial approval [20].

Demand peaks are managed by closures. For Semana Santa 2026 the city planned to disable the Centro Histórico access control on the Carretería-Álamos axis from 27 March to 6 April [6], and in 2025 some municipal car parks closed once the police cut traffic [7]. For the Feria de Málaga in August 2026 the city counted 5,066 spaces in its central car parks and 3,185 car spaces at the fairground, with several car parks open 24 hours [8]. Málaga airport handled 26.76 million passengers in 2025, up 7.4% [21]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
All nine car parks in our Málaga data, 3,780 spaces, are SMASSA car parks, which is a municipal company. Two are within 500 m of the Plaza de la Constitución, Plaza de la Marina (450) and Tejón y Rodríguez (262), and two more within 1 km. We have no price data for them, and the only published rotation tariff we found is Pío Baroja's from 2024, at €0.037 a minute for the first 30 minutes, excluding VAT [12].

Occupancy over August to early October 2026 averaged 51% on weekdays and 44% at weekends. The two central car parks are the fullest: Plaza de la Marina (75% on weekdays, 74% at weekends) and Tejón y Rodríguez (73%, 72%), which average 74% against 41% for the two between 500 m and 1 km. They are followed by El Palo (57%), Salitre and San Juan de la Cruz (both 52%) and Cervantes (48%). The emptiest are Avenida de Andalucía and Carlos Haya (both 37%). Carlos Haya drops to 22% at weekends, against 72% to 74% for the two central car parks. The data cover the summer holidays, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Málaga.
